utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Thursday, 17th July, 2008. I would like to greet the accused, their Defence counsel, the OTP representatives, as well as everybody assisting us. I will first read out an oral decision on the sealing of exhibit -- before I do so we need to move into private session because this concerns an exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's bring the witness in. Mr. Stringer, you have used up almost four hours, so you still have three hours and 15 minutes left. We're still waiting for the witness, who must be on another floor. Here he comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now give the floor to Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon also to Your Honours, counsel, all the parties and the people working in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When we finished our work yesterday we'd been talking about your visit to Zagreb and the meeting with President Tudjman which occurred in September of 1992, and then I asked you a couple brief questions about the constitutional court decision which was issued on the following day, the 18th of September, 1992. So now I'd like to move ahead to the 17th of October, 1992, which I think we'll agree was the date of the final Presidency meeting, meeting of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I know that there was a good deal of legislation that was discussed and which was enacted or approved by the Presidency in its session of 17 October 1992. The one piece of legislation that I want to talk to you about now is in your binder, it is, I think, in binder number 2, P 00684 -- I'm sorry, it's in binder 3. And, Mr. Buntic, while that document is being located by all of us, I think I said it, let me just make sure that we've established this. As we look at this document which is one of the decisions or decrees coming from the 17th of October Presidency meeting, is it true, sir, that this is the last meeting of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna until, I believe, in August of 1993, at which time the Presidency passed over its powers to the newly formed or established House of Representatives of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, looking at Exhibit P 00684, we have this as a decision on amendments to the statutory decision on the provisional organization of executive power and administration in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and I'm passing over using the word "area" or "territory." I'm going to try to be a little more -- less controversial on that subject today. I think the issue has gotten plenty of coverage in your earlier testimony. And looking at Article 1 of this decision, sir, it provides or amends the previously -- the previous decisions establishing the executive authority of the HVO, in that this provision provides that: "In the exercise of its powers the HVO may or shall adopt decrees, decisions, dispositions, and conclusions." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. It is a decision to amend -- to amend and to supplement -- well, we've already discussed this, that this decision was amended by this one. That's what I talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's right. And in Article 1 we see that definitions are given to the various forms of -- I guess -- well, we see that there are definitions that are given for the decree and a decision and a disposition and a conclusion, all of which are different types of items that can be now adopted by the HVO as part of its authority; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. This Article does, indeed, regulate all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in the second-to-last paragraph, just under the paragraph on conclusion, it states: "'In cases not suffering delay, the HVO shall adopt enactments falling been the competence of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, with the understanding that it shall be duty-bound to submit these enactments for consent to the Presidency of the HZ HB at the first session of the Presidency following the adoption of such enactments.'" Is it correct, Mr. Buntic, for us to conclude based on these passages in Article 1 that what this document does essentially is to move the legislative authority or the legislative function of the Presidency across to the HVO HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. You quoted this article correctly, but I would like to stress that these are legal instruments that were passed in cases where there could be no delays. So the purpose of those amendments was to deal with situations that are urgent or emergency, and in such cases the HVO could enact decisions and so on that were within the purview of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in fact, in the months that followed the adoption of this decision in October 1992, the HVO did in fact adopt and enact a rather substantial body of decrees and decisions. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, but if I may just make one point. These are typical situations that occurred in the state of war or imminent threat of war. The Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina passed a similar decision, transferring some of its powers on the Presidency, so the legislative transferred its powers to the executive body. The reason is because the Presidency, in our case in the Assembly in the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina, could not convene and that is why the decisions -- the power to make decisions were vested now in smaller bodies that were not so cumbersome. So that was the purpose, the objective, behind these amendments. And I can confirm as far as the second part of your question is concerned that a large body of regulations was adopted, as indicated here, decrees, decisions, dispositions, conclusions, and so on. So I believe what you say is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I believe we saw at one phase of your direct examination that at the very end of the tenure of the HVO at the time of the establishment of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, in fact all of the legislation that had been adopted by the HVO was submitted to the Presidency, which is then adopted probably as one of its final official acts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Mr. Prosecutor, and this piece of evidence was shown here in court and it was admitted in my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me, Mr. Buntic, that this particular decree, decision, does not provide that any of the legislation or enactments of the HVO is ever to be sent to the Presidency or to any of the other bodies of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina for approval?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that, but at the same time I have to make a point. All the regulations passed by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and for all practical purposes both de jure and de facto were verified or confirmed by the Washington and Dayton Accords because it was stipulated that they shall remain in force until they are replaced by federal regulations dealing with that particular sphere. To my mind, this was a verification on the part of the international community in an agreement signed by all the sides in Bosnia and Herzegovina under the auspices of the international community enshrined in the highest legal instrument in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the constitution. All those regulations were verified and confirmed, and both the Supreme Court and the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina continue to make decisions on the basis of the regulations that were passed by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So it's your testimony then that, if I understand correctly, first of all, none of the HVO legislation was sent to the government or government bodies of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that, in your view, all of the HVO's enactments were subsequently approved or accepted as part of the peace agreements, either the Washington Agreement or Dayton?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct, and I said that the signatories of those agreements were the highest bodies of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Republic of Croatia, the Republic of Serbia, the United States of America were guarantors. So all those regulations were de jure confirmed and re-affirmed, and de facto the Supreme and Constitutional Courts of Bosnia and Herzegovina continue making its decisions, basing them on those regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: However, and just so we're clear, do we agree that the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, which was the entity at the time of the Washington Agreement and Dayton, that in fact the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna did not survive and did not exist under the framework of Dayton, for example?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you say is true, but I think it would be appropriate to add that those regulations of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna were applied at the same time and equally as the regulations stemming from the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia; and it is true what you also say, that in accordance with the Washington and Dayton Peace Agreements the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was not established as such, it was part of the BH Federation. And in accordance with the Dayton Accords, Bosnia and Herzegovina was a compound state that comprised two entities, not three. One of the entities is the Republika Srpska and the other is the Federation, the Bosnian-Croat Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So I just want to take a quick step back to recap how the government or how governance in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was organized, and from this period, on the 17th of August, 1992, until August to October of 1993 when the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was declared. And I'm going to try to do this very briefly with a chart because sometimes illustrations can be more helpful. I'm going to refer to a chart that's in evidence as Exhibit P 09689, 9689, and I'm going to use Sanction. We can all look at this in Sanction, although the witness has the chart also in his binder and he can look at that in his binder because I think that will have a translated version for him. Mr. Buntic, I don't know how well you can even see this. Are you able to see the chart? Let me --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the chart, but I can't really read because the font is too small.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I put a square around the thing at the top and we can make that bigger, it says Mate Boban, president of the HZ HB and supreme commander. Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can read what I have on my screen now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And can we agree, sir, that during this period of time he was president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and he was also supreme commander of its armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the HZ HB and the supreme commander of the armed forces, but, Mr. Prosecutor, not of the state but of the community. What I heard was of the state, and this was not a state, it was a community.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in English I used the word "community," and so there may have been some misinterpretation, but I meant the HZ HB. Now, in addition, as you've testified about earlier, there was for a time during the earlier phase, Mr. Boban was also the president of the HVO, which was the executive branch, if you will.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I explained about the period. I don't know if I have to repeat what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No. And then he no longer was president of the HVO as from August of 1992 when Mr. Prlic became president of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to move over to this part of the chart which relates to the Presidency, and the language that you're seeing in English and I'll read it to you so you can get it in Croatian, under it is from the actual decree that we discussed earlier. "HZ HB Presidency 'includes representatives of the Croatian people either the top functionary in the municipal government or the president of the municipal HVO.'" So now, Mr. Buntic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this point, before he asks any more questions I'm going to object to this line of questioning for the following reasons. One, this should be translated for Mr. Buntic to look at in its entirety. I understand the concept of piecemealing, sectioning, dissecting, which can give an erroneous, global picture at the end. So that's number one. Number two, it should be translated for the gentleman. They had ample time to have it translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thirdly, it should be available to the gentleman in a hard copy. So I would object to just going step by step in this fashion because I do think it is inappropriate and it is taking advantage of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think the Trial Chamber's in a better position to judge whether we're taking advantage of the witness based on all of his testimony so far. It's my understanding that he does have in hard copy the chart in front of him, it's available certainly in the binders, as I'd indicated, and we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, this chart is in English. Could you please indicate to the witness what are the titles in this chart that you wish to see so that he can orientate himself in his own language. Maybe it's not that complicated. So I propose that you say, Here's the title, underneath you can read Mate Boban, that's what it says in English, and so on and so forth, so as to enable the witness to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would also ask, Your Honour, to give the gentleman an opportunity to study it because what's important is also the lines because obviously what we're trying to establish here - that is, the Prosecution - is some sort of command superior/subordinate responsibility by having this chart. And I suggest that the witness have an opportunity, and I would also ask where they're going to be pointing to some sort of particular box where there is a hierarchy, that is, superior/subordinate relationship, that there also be some documentation tied into it to give the gentleman an opportunity to make sure that what is being purported in this chart is also in line with any particular legislation, that would be de jure, that is. De facto they can argue whatever they want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you can provide additional information to the witness and tell him that as far as the Prosecution is concerned this is the political and military chain of command of the HZ HB, then the witness will tell you whether he agrees or not with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I'm going to use the cursor here and I'll just show you the areas that I'm going to ask you about and then you can look at those on your version and we can just take it step by step. Here I've got the -- I'm going to ask you about Mr. Boban which I've highlighted there and you can see the same part on the chart in your language. We've already covered him. I'm going to ask you about the Presidency, which I've highlighted now, which is over on this side of your chart. And I'm going to ask you about the HVO, which I've now highlighted here. And so that's what I'm going to ask you about. I'm not going to go into any of the other areas of the chart, and it's simply to try to summarize, if we can, the different competencies of these three boxes, if you will, during the period from October of 1992, the 17th of October, until the establishment of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. So are you able to follow along on your own version?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So now I was asking you about the Presidency here, and again just to -- just to confirm, the Presidency is the legislative branch of governance in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna exclusively until the 17th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minor correction. I had already clarified this. We could not call it a legislative body in the full sense of the word - I've already spoken about this. The Presidency was the highest body of control and issued regulations. We cannot call it a legislative body because it hasn't enacted a single law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So it enacted legislation -- or it enacted regulations, which I guess have different words under the decisions, decrees, decisions, conclusions, et cetera. In your view, those are all forms of regulations that were within the competency of the Presidency to issue?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Those are regulations enacted by the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And prior to the 17th of October, 1992, the HVO did not have authority to enact decrees, decisions, conclusions, et cetera, only the Presidency could do that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then after the 17th of October, 1992, that authority to issue decrees, decisions, enactments, et cetera, was given to the HVO HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It's this decision of the 17th October, whereby these powers were transferred to the HVO. And if -- those were decisions that need to be taken urgently in situations that bore no delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. But as we know, in reality what happened was that the HVO enacted scores, perhaps hundreds of decrees, decisions, et cetera, in the time that followed the 17th of October until the establishment of the Croatian Republic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, and all these regulations are described in that list that has already been exhibited in this case during my earlier testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is that the Narodni List you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I meant the list of all exhibits --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, I mentioned the Narodni List. We know that there was an Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in which much but not all of the decisions and decrees were published; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree that most of the decisions issued by the HVO were published.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it's my understanding that the HVO had the authority to decide not to publish certain decisions or decrees for reasons of security or if other justification existed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, it was wartime. There were discussions about many issues that were sensitive in nature, and publishing them during the war would have provided information to the enemy about certain things that were certainly not fit for the public. But there must have been other reasons as well. For instance, it was considered that it was not necessary to publish less important, minor regulations or decisions. There may have been third reasons as well, but I know that there were reasons why not all the decisions of the HVO were published.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. But a valid decree or decision of the HVO would still have effect even if it wasn't published; is that true? It would still have legal validity or validity under the rules that applied to HVO enactments?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the contents of the decision. In the final provisions, the decision could have said that it enters into force on the date of its issue, but the wording could also have been that it entered into force on the day of its promulgation. So there were different wordings with different legal effects.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So just to finish off this issue then, we have from October 17th, 1992, a system in which the HVO is the supreme executive and administrative body in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO HZ HB was the highest executive and controlling body, that is beyond dispute. But there was also the Presidency as the highest legislative body that could meet every day and had the possibility to accept or reject a decision made by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. But we've already established that the Presidency didn't meet anymore until the end of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So in effect, it was the HVO that was the supreme executive and it was also the only body that was issuing valid enactments, decrees, decisions, et cetera, on behalf of the governance of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer yes. I'd rather stand by my previous answer. The supreme administrative body continued to be the Presidency of the HZ HB, which could still meet every day and reject or render invalid any decision made by the HVO. It had those powers and those powers follow clearly from all decisions including this decision of the 18th October, whereby the decision -- whereby the Presidency remains the supreme body with the power of invalidating any decision made by the HVO. So I can't accept that the HVO was the highest body of control and administration because -- because the Presidency remained in that role, including by virtue of the decision of the 17th October.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you then, setting aside the de jure function and authorities then. In practice in terms of what actually happened for about one year, from October of 1992 until about October 1993, the Presidency did not meet. The HVO enacted decisions and decrees and the Presidency did not nullify any of the decisions or decrees issued by the HVO during that time. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say yes if you phrase it that way, but I stand by my previous answer to the previous question as phrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, also at the October 1992 Presidency meeting, this is when we see the appointment of Messrs. Valenta, Zubak, and Ivanovic, I believe, as vice-presidents of the HVO HZ HB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct, but in interpretation I heard Jovanovic. It's not Jovanovic, it's Ivanovic, with an I. Valenta, Zubak and Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And it's my understanding that those gentlemen were selected at least in part on the basis of the fact that they were living or came from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina so that they could balance out or fill out, if you will, from a geographic point of view the composition of the HVO; Mr. Valenta being from Central Bosnia, Mr. Zubak also being from -- certainly outside of western Herzegovina. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only outside of Herzegovina, but also outside the hitherto area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, because if we read carefully the transcript of that session you will see that in that session the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I'm sorry. Mr. Pusic doesn't seem to be feeling well. If you would allow him to leave the courtroom temporarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem. Do you want us to call a doctor? Mr. Registrar, can you please ask the Tribunal's doctor to come and see the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were indicating that I believe the composition of the vice-presidents was not only from beyond western Herzegovina but was also beyond the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as well.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, because we see from the rest of the record -- in fact we will see at that session the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was joined by the community of Usora from which Zubak came from, the community Soli, and the community Bosnian Posavina, so areas that had not been in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna until then and which joined at that session. Accordingly, vice-presidents of the HVO were appointed from various parts, various areas. Mr. Zubak from Usora, Mr. Anto Valenta from the area of Travnik, and Mr. Ivanovic, I can't remember this minute, perhaps it will come back in five minutes, I can't remember the locality, so they were outside this of area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another topic unless the Trial Chamber has questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I want to direct you to the next exhibit now which is one we've looked at already P 00303, which is in binder number 1. This is the statutory decision on temporary organization of the executive authority administration in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This is the decision of 3 July 1992. We looked at this already but now I want to ask you about some other parts of this, specifically in Articles 13, 14, and 15. This relates to the relationship between the HVO HZ HB and to the other administrative bodies, specifically the municipal bodies. Now, in Article 13 we see here that the HVO has the right and the duty to annul a regulation passed by a department or administrative body which is detrimental to the general interest or contravenes established policy. Article 14 states that the HVO shall supervise the work of its departments and municipal HVOs and that the HVO may use its supervisory powers to annul or abolish individual legal acts passed by the bodies referred to in the foregoing paragraph so that the HVO could annul or abolish individual legal acts by its departments and also by municipal HVOs. And then Article 15 states that: "If a municipal HVO has passed a decision or performed an act violating basic legal provisions of the HZ HB, the HVO has the right and the duty to dissolve the said municipal HVO ..." At which time, if I can paraphrase, the mandate of any such HVO members would be -- would cease to exist. So the point of this, Mr. Buntic, is the following. Would you agree with me, sir, that the HVO HZ HB did under its legislation or under this decree, decision, have the authority to annul or to nullify enactments coming from the municipal HVOs which it thought were inappropriate or were unlawful?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the provisions you have almost quoted from, faithfully enough, it would seem to follow that the HVO had such powers, it had such powers de jure. But it's questionable whether de facto it was able to function like that, because as you know in the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna there were representatives of municipalities and the HVO was answerable to the Presidency as the supreme body. It's true that the regulations stipulated that, but in practice it couldn't function that way because it was precisely the representatives of municipalities that sat on the Presidency, the supreme body, were able to replace the HVO as a whole or in part or any of its individual members and thus de facto disable the implementation of any provision adopted by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I was going to ask you about that. You mentioned this earlier, this tension that existed in the legislation. It seems to me, sir, that on a de facto level, the fact that the Presidency never met anymore after the 17th of October, 1992, indicates to me, sir, that it was in agreement with or certainly didn't have any serious dispute with the legislation or the enactments, I should say, of the HVO. I mean, in fact and from a de facto point of view, there doesn't seem to have been any tension. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you read the transcripts from that period carefully we can find a series of cautions at HVO sessions, not only by one representative but by many including the chairman, the president, indicating the need to convene a session of the Presidency. So I wouldn't like it interpreted, nor is it possible to interpret, that the HVO grabbed power that rightfully belonged to the Presidency and that it was not in the HVO's interests for the Presidency to convene. Because we've seen from a number of records and conclusions made by the HVO that people warned of this, they called for sessions of the Presidency, conclusions were adopted that the Presidency should meet urgently, but the HVO could not bring that about or convene the session of the Presidency itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we'll see that in the minutes, but my point actually is the opposite. I agree with you. I've seen indications in the HVO minutes of a wish or a desire that the Presidency would meet. What I don't see is any indication that the Presidency felt the need to meet. And if that's the case, it seems to me that there wasn't the tension that you describe in which the HVO felt that the Presidency was unhappy or was disapproving of the enactments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Buntic, before you answer. The question is asking for the witness to speculate. Look at the question quite carefully. How can Mr. Buntic say with any degree of certainty what the Presidency - because we're talking about various municipalities, not some monolithic entity - how could he possibly answer that question? Now, if he wants to go municipality by municipality, that's fine, but he's asking the gentleman to speculate based on his theory that since they didn't meet ipso facto, they agreed with what the HVO was doing, and so on and so forth. I think it calls for speculation, he cannot possibly answer that question, and I don't think it's helpful to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, if the witness can't answer the question, he's perfectly capable of telling us so. The witness is a lawyer and let him answer the question. You get on your feet as if the witness was completely illiterate, uneducated, but I believe that he's perfectly capable of answering the question, considering the senior position he held. He is perfectly aware of the level of speculation entailed by a given question. If we had a farmer from Arkansas in front of us that would be quite a different matter, but we're not dealing with a farmer from Arkansas here, we are dealing with someone who held senior responsibilities, someone who is a lawyer just like you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- I take your point. It wasn't meant to be. I am entitled to make my record and I'm not trying to demean the witness, obviously, but it does put him in a position where if he is combative with the Prosecution, it gives the impression to the Trial Chamber that he's being less than forthright. So he has a role to play and I have a role to play, but I do take your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like only to add, that although I agree with the argumentation of our Presiding Judge, Judge Antonetti, at the same time I have to tell you that I did meet a good number of Arkansas farmers and they are really very nice and really very educated persons as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should have used the example of a French farmer; we wouldn't have had any problem then. Fine, Mr. Stringer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not from Arkansas, Mr. President, I just want you to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I'm going to -- I'll state the question again. I think it's, I may say, a fair question based on this tension as I've described it in the legislation and which you've brought to the Trial Chamber's attention. We agree that on paper the Presidency had a position of supremacy in respect of the HVO. However, we also know that after the 17th of October the Presidency didn't meet anymore and it didn't nullify any of the enactments of the HVO. So it seems to me, sir, that in practice the reality was that the tension you have described for us did not exist. Can you comment on that? Was the Presidency, based on what you know and what you saw, unhappy or disapproving of the enactments and the work of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered in part, by saying that the HVO had no tools, no way to convene a session of the Presidency. I also said that there were representatives of as many as 40 different localities sitting on the Presidency at a later stage. I don't know the individual positions of various members of the Presidency on the work of the HVO, it would be pure guess-work. But one thing is certain, they had more than one single opinion and they had different positions on the decisions of the HVO in various municipalities. And there are indications that certain municipalities did not follow the regulations enacted by the HVO at all. They issued their own regulations which were completely contrary to what the HVO described. There are a number of examples, and I believe some of them are in the exhibits already shown. And if we were to make an analysis, I believe you can find a lot of evidence that the municipalities did not consistently implement the regulations enacted by the HVO, they issued their own regulations that ran counter to the HVO ones. I've said a lot about this, but this is all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Isn't it also true, however, that the HVO HZ HB enacted decisions nullifying municipal HVO legislation pursuant to this decision we've just been looking at?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question is correct now. There were such examples. I don't think there were that many. And I'm sure that there were many more examples of municipalities passing decisions or regulations that were contrary to the regulations enacted by the HVO, but the HVO did not annul them or revoke them. So I think that now we have a full picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then let's move on to the next exhibit, which is P 00250, it should be in the same binder, 250. This is the statutory decision on municipal executive authority and municipal administration. This is one of the earlier decrees. It's from 13 June 1992. Now, what this does, Mr. Buntic, can we agree that, looking at Article 1, that this decision provides that: "Executive authority falling within the rights and obligations of the municipality shall be exercised by the municipal HVO"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that: "The municipal HVO," looking at Article 2, "shall consist of its president, heads of office, and other members who shall be appointed and dismissed by the HVO HZ HB"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, you can see that in Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just focusing on those two articles then, am I correct, sir, that the gist of this decision is to say that things that -- the competencies that were previously within the competency of the municipality are now going to be executed at the municipality level by the municipal HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 2 stipulates the structure of the municipal HVO, what it comprises, not its jurisdiction. And I couldn't agree with you when you say that Article 2 stipulates that the municipal HVOs shall take over tasks that were within the purview of the municipalities, that does not follow from this article. What follows from this article is the structure of the municipal HVOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm -- let's look at Article 1 again then. Doesn't this mean, sir, that the executive authority at the level of the municipality is to be exercised by the municipal HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this question calls for a clarification of the first article, Article 1. So we had the pre-war structure of the government and municipality. When we looked at that, we saw that the government at the municipal level consisted of the Municipal Assembly, which was the highest administrative body in the municipality or the body of governance. It passed various enactments, and in addition to the Municipal Assembly, there was also the Executive Council of the municipality which dealt with executive matters. So the executive body was the Executive Council of the municipality, and we had this structure in place in each and every municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina and probably throughout Yugoslavia. Article 1 does not mean that the tasks from the purview of the Municipal Assembly shall be taken over, but tasks from the purview of the municipal Executive Council. So the municipal HVO, in the sense of Article 1, actually replaces the Executive Council of the municipality, not the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me, sir, that Article 1 doesn't make such a distinction, and that it in fact quite broadly and clearly states that: "Executive authority falling within the rights and obligations of the municipality shall be exercised by the municipal HVO." It doesn't specify Municipal Assembly or Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well -- but it is quite obvious that we are talking about the executive government because the second word you see "executive authority that falls within the rights and obligations of the municipality ..." and that means the Executive Council because executive authority, executive matters, were dealt with by the Executive Council. And to my mind this definition is quite clear. There are no dilemmas here. It's uncontroversial. It is quite clear that we're talking about the tasks related to the executive government in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in June of 1992 when this decision was issued, I believe that in your municipality of Citluk you didn't have a Municipal Assembly by that point, but in fact you had something else called a Crisis Staff. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June 1992, I think that the Municipal Assembly did function, that it did meet; and as for the matters that fell within the Executive Council of the Citluk municipality, those matters were dealt with by the Citluk Crisis Staff. So the executive power or the executive matters because the Municipal Assembly of the Citluk municipality was in a position, had the power, to dissolve the Crisis Staff of Citluk. The Assembly appointed members of the Crisis Staff and it could dissolve it at any moment. So it functioned at that time, which does not mean that the state of affairs prevailed in all the municipalities. It depended on the extent to which they were embroiled in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So then it's your testimony, sir, that under this decision it was the municipal HVOs that would then assume the authority or the competencies exercised previously by the Executive Councils of the various municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of Article 1 of this decision, this is the conclusion that follows without any doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And these would be the municipalities listed in Article 2 of the amended decision, or also the original decision, proclaiming the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've already said that. Municipalities or certain parts of those municipalities, there has been quite a lot of discussion about that yesterday, and other communities that joined the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now -- and I agree with you, we've heard plenty about this already. Article 1 does not make a reference to parts of municipalities, Croatian parts, Muslim parts. It simply says "the municipality." So this is my question, because we know what your views are on this: Is it possible that someone, say up in Gornji Vakuf or Kiseljak or Jablanica or any of the other 30 municipalities that are listed in the original decision, the decree, that someone up there in one of those municipalities could just -- might interpret this as establishing authority for the HVO to take executive control over the entire municipality, not a part?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we saw different cases. So if we want to go back to the structure of military units, we talked about that, we said that in the Mostar municipality in particular or throughout Herzegovina in the initial area -- in the initial period there were 30 per cent Bosniaks in the HVO units. We talked about the insignia and the emblems that those soldiers wore. I failed to mention I guess something yesterday, something that is quite important --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that is that it was tolerated. Yes, you're excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for not allowing you to finish, but I'm going to insist that you stay with me in my questions. Counsel will have an opportunity to ask you more questions on re-direct. I'm sure you'll ultimately have an opportunity to say whatever it is you like, but I've got to hold you to my questions. Like all the other attorneys, I've got time limitations and so we've got to stay on topic. So the question is this, and I'll put it a different way: Isn't it true, sir, that throughout the many municipalities listed in Article 2 of the original decree establishing Herceg-Bosna, that this and other legislation of the HVO was interpreted to mean or provide for a complete take-over of the executive authority of the entire municipality? Isn't that how it actually worked on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, just one explanation if you deem it to be of any use. I think that the witness really cannot understand this question, and if I may indicate why. That's because in Article 1 of this decision we're not talking about the territory, area, or whatever of the municipality, but the rights and obligations of the municipality which may be exercised over a small or large area. And I think this is why the Prosecution and the witness appear to be at odds. I'm -- I would be glad if I could really help you with this explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I thought it might be an interpretation problem. Could you read out Article 1 in your language. Could you read out Article 1 and this will be translated by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, this is all about my attitude towards the Prosecutor and his way of asking questions. And if I may be given one minute to say something about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you prefer, but I was interested mostly in Article 1. What did you want to say, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to say that in the course of my testimony here over 500 documents were shown to me containing over 5.000 pages. I was asked to provide short answers, and later on there were objections criticising me why I failed to provide a full answer to some questions. Today and yesterday I am often interrupted by the Prosecution in the middle of my train of thought. I have the right to protest against that. I am not opposed to the Prosecution asking questions, but I have to protest against being interrupted in the middle of my sentence. These are not yes or no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you please read out Article 1, and this will be deducted from the time allocated to the Bench. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Article 1: "Tasks pertaining to the executive authority within the framework of the rights and obligations of the municipality shall be carried out by the municipal Croatian Defence Council (hereafter: The municipal HVO)."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Suppose we have a municipality predominantly inhabited by Muslims. According to this text would municipal authority be delegated to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, until the Croat-Bosniak conflict broke out, there never had been any problems about the area where the HVO was operating and the area where the Crisis Staffs set up by the army or the Presidency or the Territorial Defence were set up. So what I wanted to say, of the members that were in the HVO units, it often happened that Bosniaks would wear the Croatian emblem and the HVO patch on one sleeve and the lily on the other, wearing green berets on their heads, and this was tolerated. It functioned well. There were no problems. Problems occurred the moment when the BH army and the HVO clashed. So in the initial period the recognition of the HVO or of decisions passed by the HVO were never forced on anyone or any municipality. The regulation stands here and it is completely uncontroversial in its Article 1. It does not cover any territory, any area, it does not pertain to any area. And perhaps I should add that the Mostar municipality HVO had in its ranks the equal proportion of Croats and Bosniaks. Such an agreement was achieved at the level of the Mostar municipality between the SDA and the HDZ. So the HVO performed tasks of the Executive Council with the equal participation of Croats and Bosniaks 50/50. So I cannot really give you a yes or no answer to what the Prosecution has asked me. I hope that now you see why I asked for this clarification to be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The example of Mostar is particularly welcome. So if it was 50/50 in Mostar, if there were as many Croats as Bosniaks, we would have to look at the latest election results. But now the Executive Council pursuant to this text is now in the HVO's hands. So the Muslims play a certain role, but from then on can they still play a role because in this text it is the HVO that is mentioned? Here's my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this text again pertains only to the executive body of the municipality. So the Municipal Assembly in Mostar continued to function and its composition was the same as it used to be before the war, and the executive tasks were assumed by the HVO which had the equal representation of Croats and Muslims 50/50. The situation was similar in other municipalities. In some municipalities it was possible for Bosniaks to participate in the HVO, in some municipalities it was not possible, and in those municipalities the HVO functioned only in part of those municipalities. This is how it functioned de facto, and this follows from this decision because there's no mention of borders, territories, areas, this is only about an executive body of the municipality in Article 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We're a bit back with something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- you told us yesterday, Mr. Buntic. I would like you to tell me who was -- what was the executive for the part of the municipality which did not belong to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was the Crisis Staff set up by the Muslims. It was called the Staff, the Bosniaks called it the Crisis Staff, and using the term "stab" and in the other part of the municipality it was the Crisis "stozer." It is the Croatian word for staff, and in most cases that's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just added something. In a municipality if you have 50/50 or 40/60 in the Assembly -- never mind. Pursuant to this text, the executive will be exercised by the HVO, but you seem to state that the Bosniaks at their own level could also set up their own Crisis Staff. So in that case we would have two structures in parallel. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. That was one of the possibilities, and it actually happened in real life. One possibility was the 50/50 representation as it was in Mostar, another possibility was to have the crisis "stab," staff, set up by Muslims in part of the municipality and Croats would set up their own Crisis Staff in the other part. And you have seen that in Tuzla and in Usora you had such a situation with the crisis "stozer" in one part of the municipality and the crisis "stab" in the other part of the municipality. And this was what happened in actual fact, and those were the actual options.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, this text only aims to organize the structure for the Croats and the HVO and does not apply to the Muslims who have their own structure; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you could interpret it this way, but we have the example of Mostar where both parties participated in the work of the same executive body. I think that there were some other areas apart from Mostar where this is how it was, but I'm sure about Mostar at any rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what happened in Citluk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for Citluk, 90 -- 99 per cent, something, of the population was Croats. So the HVO was structured to reflect proportionately the composition of the population, and there were some other examples where Bosniaks, Muslims, participated in the work of the HVO. Just to give you an example, in the judiciary of Bosnia and Herzegovina there were over 40 per cent of the Bosniak, Muslims, although --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise, could the witness please repeat the percentage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm looking at the clock, I think it might be time to have the first break. It's 20 to 4.00. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back in session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, just to stay with this Exhibit, P 00250, a little bit longer, you were answering some questions of the Judges before the break. And if I understood you correctly, you had indicated, if I can put it this way, there were two possibilities for the municipalities. I suppose one could --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise. Before the question's put, just before the adjournment the interpreters did state that they didn't manage to get the translation, so perhaps -- it's page 32, lines 19 and 20. Perhaps that could be clarified before we go on to some new substantive matter or further matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President, and I meant to raise that. I forgot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, just before the break you were talking about the percentages of participation. I'm looking at the transcript. You're talking about where Bosniaks, Muslims, participated in the work of the HVO. And then you were giving an example in the judiciary of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I think you indicated that there were over 40 per cent of Bosniak Muslims, but then there was a break and the interpreters indicated that they were not, they did not pick up the percentage that you had indicated there. So is it possible for you to just continue that thought or restate what your testimony was about the level of participation of Bosniak Muslims in the judiciary in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that participation was higher than 40 percentage, and at any rate, it was higher than the relative proportion of Bosniaks in the territory of HZ HB. I can use an example of the municipal court of Mostar, where for the duration of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna there were eight judges, Bosniaks; four Croat judges; and one Serb. So that was the composition of the municipal court. At the higher court in Mostar there were eight Bosniaks, six Croats, and two Serbs, which tells us that the Judges, too, continued to work in the courts of HZ HB. There was no racial discrimination and there were no problems on that score until the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, getting back to this Exhibit, P 00250. If I understand your testimony correctly, you indicate that there were two frameworks, if you will, through which one could participate in the governance of a municipality. One would have been through the municipal HVO framework, where you indicated, I think, there was an alternative that was used in some of the more Bosniak municipalities which was the Crisis Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that such possibilities de facto occurred and operated on the ground. That was one option that existed de facto and was implemented in the territory of the HZ HB, but also outside that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm talking about within the HZ HB then. It sounds to me as though we're talking about parallel authorities, if you will, existing side by side, both of which are exerting jurisdiction or authority over what is probably going to be the same territory. Was that the situation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat again that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna did not have borders. Its territory was not defined. All the time it was called a locality, an area, and that's how it was defined in the decision to establish it. But I also described how it worked in reality, that there were various options, various possibilities in various municipalities, we had different structures. I said it was correct that in principle it worked that way in the area of a certain mixed municipality Bosniak/Croat. The HVO operated in one part of that municipality's territory, whereas in another part of that territory there was a Crisis Staff or the municipal War Presidency, depending on how the other side called it. In practice different names were used, and today speaking about it, it's hard to find one single uniform name because in the documents we've seen we see that in some places it was called the Territorial Defence Staff, in other places it was called the Crisis Staff, in some places it was called the War Presidency, in yet others it was called the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please allow me to finish --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think you have given a full and sufficient answer if I may say so, Mr. Buntic. The picture you paint, if I may say so, sounds rather harmonious, a picture in which the various executive authorities in the various municipalities all operate simultaneously within what everyone apparently understands to be his own defined area of jurisdiction and that there were no clashes or disputes about which authority could actually legitimately claim to exercise authority over a given area. Isn't that how it really was, there was tremendous tension as time went on between HVO municipal authorities on the one hand and other Muslim or Crisis Staff authorities on the other?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. After a while that state of affairs through a natural course of things led to a conflict. The conflict between Croats and Bosniaks occurred when the Muslim or the Bosniak side, using the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and security services, tried forcibly with its army and its police to implement the decree on districts, that's something that the Bosniak side accepted as its own arrangement. After the Vance-Owen Plan which was accepted by both sides, the Croats and Bosniaks accepted the provinces as defined in the Vance-Owen Plan which were not the same as districts, that is when the conflict occurred, when each side tried to impose their own arrangements. The Croats -- you're interrupting me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I asked you whether there was conflict or whether there was harmony. I didn't ask you, sir, with respect, to give us your views on what was the event which triggered the conflict. Can we agree that there was tension or is it your testimony there was harmony? I'm not asking you about the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, if I may. I believe the Prosecution, or rather, my learned friend came to the crucial issue, the most important issue of all, and now when the witness wants to give a complete answer he is not allowed to do so. We are not going to learn the whole story or at least Mr. Karnavas will have to do an extensive re-direct. I believe this witness should be allowed to fully explain his theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the problem is that the Prosecutor has been allocated a certain amount of time, he has his own case, his own strategy, he's prepared a number of questions, and he's trying to control the answers of the witness as far as possible. As part of re-direct you may decide to come back to the issue of harmony or tension, but what the Prosecutor was trying to find out is whether there was tension or harmony or not. And the answer we got is that there was no harmony. Now, of course we could spend hours trying to identify the cause of this lack of harmony. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I based my intervention primarily on the question as it was asked, and the question precisely sought the answer that the witness provided. The first part of the answer is strictly within the question; and the second part of the answer, when the witness started to elaborate why it was so, like: Is it white? Yes, it is white because ... and that's the point where the Prosecution no longer finds it convenient to let the witness continue. One of the most important characteristic of your guidance is that you gave some lenience. We did not stick to the strict common-law system. As long as the witness is answering the question, and I believe he is, he should be allowed to complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Kovacic, I can remember that the style when the witnesses were brought by the Prosecution, and I can very well imagine how the Defence would have reacted if in their cross-examination they would have had advice from the Prosecutor which questions they should ask and what answers they should wait for. I think this is now cross-examination, and I'm sure the Prosecution, Mr. Stringer, has some plan and I don't think it is for the witness or for the Defence to make him depart from that. There is a period of re-direct when the Defence can straighten all this out. But we have heard this witness and he has a tendency to give very long and copious answers. And I think Mr. Stringer has been patient on the whole and we should leave him continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely the point: The Prosecution has its plan. Of course they have their plan, at least I do hope so and I expect of a colleague of this rank to have a plan. And it is a part of that plan to refuse a no answer, not to allow a no answer. I did not in any way influence the phrasing of the question. The question was asked, the answer was given, and I got to my feet only after the witness was interrupted. So it never crossed my mind to suggest to my learned friend how to ask the question. He formulated the question the way he wanted to, and the question calls for this answer. But let us go back to the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you may proceed. If the Judges feel that we need to explore that issue further, we'll do so. As you have seen previously, sometimes questions are asked by the Bench and these questions suit neither the Defence nor the Prosecution because we believe that a given matter should be explored further. Yes, of course about the harmony or lack of harmony, we could try to identify the reasons for this, the cause for this. But that may take quite a lot of time. So it probably best to leave it at that. So please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will. I intervene after some 10 or 12 lines of the answer because I think the witness actually did answer my question very succinctly at the very beginning. He agreed with me, he said: "That's correct." Now, he went on to talk about how that led to the war and who, in his view, was responsible for starting the war. I do believe that was beyond the scope of my question and that's why I intervened when I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, let me just pass over to the next topic and I'm going to direct you to Exhibit P 00449, which is in binder number 2. Mr. Buntic, I believe you testified about this document before. I think I can correctly state that it would have fallen within -- it was among the various decrees that you were involved in in your capacity as head of the justice department. This is the decree on application of the criminal code of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also the criminal code of the former Yugoslavia. On the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, it's a long name for a decree. If I understand correctly, this is the decree by which the criminal codes of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of the former Yugoslavia then were enacted and applied to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My question on this is as follows. This decree is dated the 14th of August, 1992, it becomes effective on the date of its publication -- I'm sorry, I believe it -- yes, it becomes effective on the same day as its enactment. On what day did the criminal code of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina no longer apply in Herceg-Bosna, such that it was necessary for this criminal code to be positively enacted into law? I can try to restate that because I may not have asked it very clearly. Here is a decree that says the criminal code of Bosnia-Herzegovina applies in Herceg-Bosna beginning today, 14th of October, 1992. That suggests to me that there was a time, say on the 13th of August, when the criminal code of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not apply, otherwise why would it be necessary to enact such a decree. So tell us, when did the criminal code of Bosnia-Herzegovina stop applying in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is never. The criminal code of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the criminal code of Yugoslavia never stopped to be applied in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and we can see from this decree that only one provision of that law, of that code, was modified; namely, the monetary amounts that were denoted in Yugoslav dinars were converted into a different currency. Nothing else was changed in the criminal codes of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, Yugoslavia. Everything was taken over, adopted, as was -- except for this little intervention and I've already explained why this single intervention was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me, sir, there would not have been a need to take this over, as you say, if it remained in effect throughout. It seems self-evident to me that the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina applied, so why is it necessary to take this over?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the same reason that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted the criminal code of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I think the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopt the Yugoslavia code because it was now a new state entity. I mean -- and let me put that to you. It seems to me that this decision or this decree implies that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna thinks it is a new form of entity such that it is necessary to adopt or to accede to other forms of legislation that had previously applied in the territory.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This wording was used in the enactment of all regulations, in cases when an intervention was needed in existing regulations, the regulation was first taken over in its entirety and then a modification was made to only that part which needed to be modified. So I don't see anything special about this decree compared to any other decree or the technique applied throughout the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. There is nothing peculiar about this decree that would not be found in any other decree. I've told you already that this was done the way it was, and I said why.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just one last point on this one. You indicated yesterday, I believe, that after April of 1992 the Official Gazettes of Bosnia-Herzegovina were not available to you unless somebody was able to smuggle them out of Sarajevo. I note that this decree refers to some of the legislation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated June of 1992. So my question is whether on the 14th of August, 1992, on the date this decree was enacted you and others in Herceg-Bosna did have, in fact, access at least to these parts of the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a claim in your question that I cannot accept. I did not say that they were smuggled out. That's the interpretation that I received. I don't know what interpretation the others received, but that's not what I said. I don't know whether this is a misinterpretation. I said unless somebody managed to get a copy of the Official Gazette of Bosnia and Herzegovina by one means or another. I think that in this specific case Mr. Zoran Perkovic, who managed to get out of Sarajevo immediately before this period and he had worked in the republican justice ministry as an assistant, he managed to bring with him a certain number of copies of the Official Gazette. He was aware as a lawyer of the importance of the Official Gazette, so sometime in July or I don't know when, it must have been the end of July, he managed to leave Sarajevo and he continued working in Mostar and he managed to get a certain number of copies of the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So if you said April of 1992 yesterday, sir, would we change that then to move that forward to June, July, August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is beyond the scope of any decency in asking a question --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I object to that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no, he says "so." He's trying to draw a conclusion. He can save that for his closing argument. He indicated that Mr. Perkovic, who was about to testify this week, had managed to go to Sarajevo and then left Sarajevo on or about June. That -- and then with him he brought the Official Gazettes. When Mr. Perkovic comes here he will testify to that trip and he will testify as to the details and he's the one that was drafting the legislation. So the conclusion that is being drawn here, one, is false; and two, is improper. And I will stand up and I will object to these sort of tactics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The witness testified that he didn't have access to the Official Gazettes after April of 1992. I've shown him the document, it's dated August of 1992 and makes explicit reference to the Official Gazettes of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least from June of 1992. I asked the witness if he wanted to modify his testimony on the basis of having seen this document. It's entirely appropriate to bring this inconsistency to the witness's attention and to offer him the opportunity to modify his testimony. That's what I've done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't want to drag things out. Of course my learned friend is perfectly entitled to put fair cross-examination and I know he's endeavouring to do that. However, perhaps it would be useful to have recourse to yesterday's transcript and I may be wrong, but it is my recollection that perhaps a distinction was drawn between the official means of receiving the Official Gazette and an ad hoc arrangement whereby the odd copy may get into the hands of the witness or get into the hands of the area concerned. So, Your Honour, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the witness can shed some light on that matter. Witness, yesterday I asked you a question about that. You stated that the Official Gazette of Bosnia and Herzegovina could not arrive in Mostar because of the situation and so on and so forth. We have here a document signed by Mr. Boban dated 14 August 1992. Mention is made of Official Gazette 3/92. There must be an explanation that you can provide.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I provided an explanation, and I maintain what I said yesterday, every word. It is true that after April 1992 we were not able to receive the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina by official courier or mail. The only exception was when somebody was able to bring it using different means, and this is what happened in this case. There was this person who brought with him just a certain number of copies of the Official Gazette. So I still stand by what I said yesterday and what I said now, and there is no contradiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, if you could turn to the next exhibit, please, it's P 01760, 1760. And this is an -- also a decree related to the application of the criminal law and also the Law on Criminal Procedure, I believe. And this one is signed by Mr. Prlic on the 18th of March, 1993, and appears to have been published on the 31st of March, 1993. And a couple of questions just about this one. The -- a number of the articles in this decree relate to changing the numbers in various parts of the criminal codes. Can we correctly assume that these are references to fines, that is, monetary penalties, that are found throughout the criminal code that would apply in the case of certain criminal violations? I'm looking at Article 2 and thereafter.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the changes in the numbers are rather dramatic. Just looking at item number 1 under Article 2, it's changing 200 into the number of 12.000, 50.000 is changed to the number of 3 million. Is this a reflection of the inflation that was taking place and its impact on the Croatian dinar at this period of time, in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not inflation that affected only the Croatian dinar. It was a galloping, hyperinflation that affected both the Yugoslav dinar -- or rather, the situation was the most serious for the Yugoslav dinar and less serious for the Croatian dinar. But it did affect both currencies. I think that in 1989 the inflation rate was 11.000 per cent. It was on the average 1 or 2 per cent a day. Financial experts will be talking about that, but there was hyperinflation of the Yugoslav dinar and substantial inflation for the Croatian dinar, and this is why the figures were higher. So we're talking about millions and this seems like a huge amount. I know that this was not the case, but we should best leave this for the financial experts. They can make an estimate as to the relative value in euros. But I couldn't give you a valuation to tell you how much it was worth in euros.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll accept that. If I could direct your attention to Article 1, there are a few more references to the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which I think the name of it is the Sluzbeni list if I'm not mistaken. Do you see a reference to the Sluzbeni list of RBiH number 6/92, dated the 15th of June, 1992, and then there's another reference to one that's dated the 1st of August, 1992. Then I'm moving down about six or seven lines. There's a reference to Sluzbeni list RBiH, again 15th of June, 1992, another one dated 12th of July, 1992. Now, this is March of 1993 that Dr. Prlic is signing this decree. Would that indicate that in March of 1993 you and the others who were drafting the legislation had access to the Sluzbeni List of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that time except in the way that I described yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to turn to the next exhibit, Mr. Buntic, it's P 00589. 00589. It is in binder number 3, and this is the decree on establishing an office of the Supreme Court on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I think I can safely use the word "territory" because that's the word that appears in the original language version. P 00589. Mr. Buntic, you've talked a lot already about the establishment of this office of the Supreme Court, and I've just got a couple of questions for you on this topic and this decree. If I could direct you -- first of all, you were involved in drafting this decree or in writing it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. If you would look at Article 5, this provides that: "The president and the judges of the office are to be elected by the Presidency of the HZ HB upon recommendation of the head of the department of defence of the HVO HZ HB."
