And we can see at the bottom that this decree is dated the 17th of October, 1992. So we know that after this day the Presidency of the HZ HB didn't meet anymore, and so can we correctly assume then that the authority to elect the presidents -- sorry, the president and judges of this office of the Supreme Court, that the authority to elect those passed from the Presidency to the HVO itself, or that in fact that authority was exercised by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not sure about the interpretation --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can try to --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because -- or translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase. This says that it's the Presidency who elects the president and judges of the court. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we agree that after this day, 17 October 1992, the Presidency of Herceg-Bosna didn't meet anymore, at least not for about a year?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So that in practice when it came time to elect judges to this office of the Supreme Court, was that done by the HVO HZ HB instead of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the appointments were done by the HVO of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what body made the other appointments? I'm talking about this particular court, the Supreme Court office.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- well, I'm not sure. Let me get back to what I said. We did not receive the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina regularly. I think that some of the judges were confirmed by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, some of the appointments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And if I understand correctly from your testimony earlier, and I know it related to judges in general, I had the impression that it -- despite what's said in Article 5 here about the department of defence being responsible to recommend judges, that in practice it turned out to be the department of justice that did that more often just because of its own knowledge of judges, lawyers, and their legal qualifications. Is that a -- roughly a correct understanding of how it turned out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Article 6 states that before taking up the duties of judge at this office of the Supreme Court, which is going to be in Mostar I believe, that these judges must make a solemn declaration in the presence of the president of the HZ HB and that it's the president of HZ HB who determines the text of the solemn declaration. Do you know whether, in fact, the judges who were selected or elected in fact did take this oath in front of Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All newly appointed judges that were not judges before the war and who were appointed to new posts by the decisions of the HZ HB had to take an oath or a solemn declaration because this is the usual practice. Any judge before the appointment, before taking up his duties or her duties, must take an oath. So we have to differentiate here between the judges who had been appointed to those posts before the war and whose post did not change, they remained where they had been before the war, they were not under an obligation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. And I hate to cut you off, but my question actually, I think, was a much simpler one which was simply whether -- do you know whether, in fact, the judges who were selected or elected did in fact take the oath before Mr. Boban? Did that happen? That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Newly appointed judges did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Was this just for the Supreme Court or was it for some of the other courts you talked about as well, the district courts, district military courts? All the new judges took an oath?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you had allowed me to continue my answer there would have been no need for your question. I wanted to give you an answer to that question. Yes, all newly appointed judges who were appointed by decisions of the body of the HZ HB to judicial duties had to take this oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at an earlier part of your testimony, I think on direct examination, you indicated that the HZ HB did not establish any new courts, no new civilian courts. Rather, it just took over the republican law on regular courts. Is that a correct statement of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's correct but with an addendum. I said that with the -- in addition to the office of the Supreme Court and the regular courts, and we left aside the military courts which were newly established.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So this is my question. For this Supreme Court office, why was it necessary then for Mr. Boban to determine text of what would be a new oath if, in fact, it's going to be the same court? It seems to me that the same oath would apply.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these were newly appointed judges. The earlier oath read that they should comply with the constitution and the laws of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. So it was no longer applicable. It was impossible for them to take an oath that they would comply with the constitution and the laws of their enemy, the aggressor, the occupier -- well, that was not realistic to expect them to take this oath, and I expect that you will see why this was not possible, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The judges who were appointed here by the HVO, did they have a duty to apply the decisions, enactments, and decrees that were being issued by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the next exhibit is P 0059 -- oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I would like to ask a question to the witness. I see a certain lack of logic, in the fact that on the one hand you said that judges who had been judges in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did not have to take a new oath, that is, they were accepted as judges to continue in their office although they had, as you put it, sworn loyalty to the arch enemy, whereas the new ones had to swear a distinctly different oath. Why did not every judge have to pass a new oath with new allegiance to the entity he was now serving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as you can see from the documents, or rather, the regulations, the second option was accepted. The reasons were that it was considered that if a judge remains in the post that they occupied before, that they didn't have to take an oath again because they had already made the oath on the occasion of assuming the post. But when a person is appointed to a post of a judge for the first time, even in accordance with the laws that were previously in force could not assume the duties of a judge without taking an oath. I'm just explaining to you what the thinking was at the time and why this solution was selected, because in accordance with the laws that were previously in force the judges could not assume their duties without taking an oath first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, the next exhibit is P 00589, and it should -- should be quite close to the one that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I should say 00594, so that should just be right behind the one we've just discussed. 594. Mr. Buntic, this is the decree on establishing the public prosecutor's office on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and again I think I'm safe to say it that way in English because I see the word "teritoriju" in the original language version. Now, in Article 2 of this document we see that the department of the public prosecutor must have at least two deputy republican public prosecutors, of whom one shall be in charge. And then Article 3 sets out the qualifications, I think. Article 4 indicates that it's the Presidency of the HZ HB which will appoint the deputies of the republican public -- excuse me, republican public prosecutor's office at the proposal of the head of the defence department. So would it be correct for me, sir, to suggest that it's a similar situation that we saw with the judges on the Supreme Court, that again because this is the 17th of October, 1992, what happened in practice was that the justice department proposed the deputy prosecutors because perhaps it was more in a better position to do so rather than the defence department, and that also it was the HVO HZ HB who actually approved the prosecutors instead of the Presidency? And if you don't remember, I'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do remember and I think that your question is properly asked and I can give you an answer and that's yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Article 6, then, now refers to the taking of a formal oath by the deputies of the republican public prosecutor's office, they take a formal oath before the president of the HZ HB. And again, here it's the Presidency that shall determine the text of the formal oath. Now, my question here is perhaps a little bit similar to the one that was just asked by Judge Trechsel. It appears to me that in order to be qualified or a candidate to be one of these two deputies republican public prosecutors, you have to already be a deputy republican public prosecutor, which implies to me that you've already taken an oath sufficient to discharge your duties as a public prosecutor. So the question is: Why would it be necessary now to take another oath, a different oath?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the elected deputy public prosecutors had been in those posts before. Both were newly appointed and in accordance with the -- my previous answer I actually repeat the same thing. If those were newly appointed persons, be they prosecutors or judges, they had to take an oath before taking their office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it was -- why wouldn't they ask to take the same oath as a republican public prosecutor would have taken in Sarajevo or in Tuzla or in Bihac, or was everybody taking different oaths?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no clue what it was like in Tuzla or in Bihac or in Sarajevo. I couldn't learn except in the way I described a moment ago, that is, if somebody managed to bring from Sarajevo one of those Official Gazettes, that was the only way. There was no other way. Sometimes, as I said, we managed to get hold of a number of Official Gazettes but not by mail. Not only we didn't receive them, the courts didn't receive them, nobody did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I think we've heard a lot about the Official Gazette. Maybe the question of the Prosecutor can be clarified. I'll try that. You said someone who is new to the post must pass an oath. Is someone new to a post when he passes from a lower level of the same profession to a higher level so that someone who had served his at least five years in accordance with Article 3 on a lower public prosecutor's office when he is appointed deputy, that is considered a new job and he's considered to be new for that level, as a -- let's say a municipal judge who is appointed to a district court would then also have a new post, be regarded as someone who is new to this post. Would that -- does that strike you as a correct interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, and what you say, Your Honour, is correct. In every change of duty from a lower level to a higher level or if a person did not serve before that in the prosecutor's office or in the court at all, he had to take an oath because he was assuming a new duty, that was the criteria, assuming a new duty. If he had been working as a higher court judge until then, first he had to be relieved from that duty and then by virtue of a decision appointing him judge to the Supreme Court he could assume a new duty. The same applied to prosecutors. If a prosecutor worked on the district level and then was appointed deputy republic prosecutor, he was automatically relieved from his previous duty and had to take an oath to assume his new one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, according to this document, the new judge or the new prosecutor has to take an oath or make a statement before the president of the HZ HB. To your knowledge, would a prosecutor or a judge from Zenica take an oath before President Alija Izetbegovic at the time? Talking about the area controlled by the ABiH, would you say that judges took the oath in that area as well and before whom did they do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think so. I don't think they were even able to because the judges from a division of the Supreme Court in Tuzla, in Zenica, and Bihac were physically separated. It was physically impossible for them to take an oath before President Alija Izetbegovic, and this provision that we have in our decree had its equivalent in the regulations enacted by districts, Zenica, Bihac, and Tuzla the arrangements were similar. Appointments were made at the proposal of the defence department because it was considered to be a state of war and it was considered that these were temporary divisions to operate provisionally, and appointments were made by the decision of a president of a district. And this was all a result of agreements and my discussions with Mr. Halilagic, whereby similar or identical arrangements were offered for the duration of the state of war, as on the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The districts had similar arrangements to those in Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question: How many lawyers were there in Herzegovina at the time? Can you give us a ballpark figure? There was at least one, yourself, but how many were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very few, Your Honour, certainly not enough to meet our needs at the time. And I believe it has to be emphasized that just before the war in Mostar, in the municipal court, and in the higher court there were only eight Croat judges working. I had been entrusted with a task of creating 11 judicial institutions, and I had only eight Croats at my disposal. This speaks eloquently of my problem. To use the example of Tomislavgrad municipal court, throughout the HZ HB it had only one judge; in another place there were only two judges. We had great problems filling the vacancies in Livno. Slightly better was the situation in Bosnian Posavina, where we managed to establish a full complement of civilian courts, the municipal, the higher, the military courts, but in this area of Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you have not answered my question. When you have courts, you need judges and you appointed a number of judges. But for these judges to do their work you need lawyers, defence counsel. How many of these were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In light of what I said before, the scarcity of judges, we were forced to mobilise lawyers in order to be able to fill vacancies in courts, and somehow, somehow, create preconditions for the judiciary to operate at all. So we filled vacancies simply by mobilising lawyers, there was no other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now things are much clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, the next exhibit is P 00 -- I'm sorry, P 01137, 1137, it's in binder 3. As usual, the President has anticipated my next question before I even got to it. Mr. Buntic, these are minutes of the 18th Session of the HVO held on the 15th of January, 1993. Is that the document that you have?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the president of the HVO, Dr. Prlic, was there; you were there; Mr. Valenta was there; others. I would like to direct your attention to item number 2, which is on page -- begins on page 2 at the bottom and it continues over to page 3. Because it actually relates to a draft provision on the implementation of the Law on the Legal Profession in the HZ HB. You proposed an amendment to Article 8 which related to the attorneys registered in the directory of the bar association of HZ HB, then Mr. Zubak proposed an additional amendment. And I don't have the final version of the decision here, but he's proposing an amendment that is adopted that indicates that the words "with the approval of the HVO HZ HB" are to be inserted into the text after the word "attorney." This suggests to me, sir, that the HVO HZ HB regulated the practice of law within the area or the territory of the HZ HB. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. The bar of HZ HB was established and it was later included and recognised by the bar association at the international level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, everything that is related to attorneys or lawyers I find interesting, as you can very well imagine. You just said something that I find very significant. You said that the bar association of the HZ HB was recognised internationally. Who or what are you referring to exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean the international bar association. Of course I don't have the document with me, but if the Court requires it I can submit it later. The document testifying to the recognition of the bar association of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that is, the document whereby it becomes a member of the international bar association.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We've been talking about the courts that you were involved in organizing, and I wanted to ask you, then, in order to be a lawyer and to practice in these courts that you've been testifying about in Herceg-Bosna, would one have to be a member of the Herceg-Bosna bar association in order to get rights of audience?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you could move on to item 7 in the same document, this is page 5 of the English, item 7. There are references to a number of proposals, and the one I want to ask you about is the third proposal there, that's made at the head of the judiciary and general administration department. There's a reference to Mr. Aid Gla vovic, attorney from Mostar. He's relieved of his post of the regulations commission. Mr. Zoran Perkovic then replaces Mr. Glavovic on the regulations commission. And then you move down a few lines to number 2 and you'll see that Mr. Aid Glavovic now is appointed as assistant head of the sector for the implementation of criminal violations and sanctions. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I believe you testified about Mr. Glavovic already in your direct testimony. He was an attorney from Mostar, as it's indicated here. He was a Muslim. And I believe at one point he was acting in the capacity as your deputy, if I state that correctly.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is correct except that he was a deputy. He was an assistant for the enforcement of criminal and misdemeanour sections. My deputy was Karlo Sesar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then continuing on the with the document there's a reference to a proposal by you, I take it, that's adopted and this is on the appointment and relieving from duty judges and public prosecutors in the various courts. And so we see that you were involved again in proposing and the HVO then is adopting decisions with respect to the appointments of judges and prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then it continues that: "In order for the appointed judges and public prosecutors to commence work, it is necessary to draft the text of the oath and to agree upon the exact date and place of taking the oath with the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Mate Boban, by the end of the forthcoming week." So do you know or do you recall, Mr. Buntic, if ultimately the text of the oath that's referred to here was agreed upon or was adopted by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. As you have seen, the text of the oath was determined by the president of the HZ HB and without his consent it couldn't be done. And as you can see, it was done in agreement with Mate Boban because that was his responsibility and the date of the taking of the oath had to be also agreed with him because it was taken before the president of the HZ HB, I'm talking about newly appointed judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the next exhibit is P 01264, 1264. I think it's just a few documents below. Now, these are minutes of the HVO meeting held just a week later. The last exhibit was 15th of January, 1993. This is one week later on the 22nd of January, 1993, again you're present at this HVO meeting with the others who are indicated there. And if I could direct you, Mr. Buntic, to item number 2, then, in the text of the minutes. We see here an indication that one of the various proposed oaths was actually adopted by the HVO, and then the text of the oath is actually set out in the minutes. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I'll just read it. "Formal oath" -- actually, maybe it's better or safer. Why don't you read us the text as you see it in the original language document.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Solemn declaration. "I hereby declare that I will observe the constitution in my work, the laws, and other positive regulations, that with diligent work I will protect the interests and the state system of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that I will perform my duty and tasks conscientiously. "As God as my witness."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Buntic, whether this is the actual text of the oath that was administered to the judges as you've indicated took place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see from the minutes, three variants were on the table; this is the one that was adopted and this is the text of the solemn oath given by judges before they assumed their role as judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, is it possible, sir, that a person who's a Muslim would be reluctant to swear this oath, as its written particularly with the reference to God, "Bog" in your language, as it's written there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have spoken about it already before this Court. It was agreed previously that instead of saying "God" they would say "Allah" and everything else was the same. There was no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next document is P 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what about the Muslim judges? You said there were some Muslim judges, so when they took the oath they said "Allah." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time of the federal republic when the oath was taken, was any reference made to a God? I don't believe it was the case, but was there such a reference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whoever would mention him would end up in prison the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what about a judge who would be an atheist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody made any problem about that either. He could keep silent about that. We had some Croat judges and Bosniak judges taking oaths, as well as atheists, and it was said that no problem would be made about this, no fuss, but some sort of oath had to be taken. Originally three variants were proposed, this one was adopted. This one was adopted without making any problem about this, but no problem was made either if somebody didn't take an oath at all; they still continued in their positions. But this was a customary procedure, in many other countries as well. We had to have some sort of text. Three versions were on the table, but no fuss was made if somebody said "Allah" instead of "God" or if they said nothing at all or even if they did not come to take the solemn oath at all. None of the judges was dismissed for that reason. They continued in their office as if nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now we're talking about judges here, the text of the judges, but it's true, isn't it, that others were required to take oaths, either the prosecutors as we've seen, and others such as members of your department, the justice and general administration department. Were employees and workers within the HVO also required to take oaths?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said before, prosecutors were required to do it but I don't know whether it was required of any other employee in my division, in my department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, if you would turn --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not denying but this would be the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps he could restate his answer. I'm told that he's indicated something other than what was translated. Perhaps he wasn't heard properly, but if he could repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you give us that answer again, please, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of prosecutors and judges who were newly appointed it was required to take a solemn oath, as was customary. But I do not know of a single example that any official in any employment department would be required to do the same. I don't know of any such case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We've -- you've mentioned and I've mentioned also now Mr. Aid Glavovic. Is it true, sir, that in fact he resigned this position as deputy in the justice department because he declined to take an oath?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Aid Glavovic had to take an oath, that's lunacy. I don't know that he was required or that he was obliged to take an oath. Of course it is your right to take -- to ask any question that comes to your mind, but this is -- it's inadmissible and it didn't exist, simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you don't know if he resigned rather than take an oath?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, Aid Glavovic was appointed my assistant. He was a correct person. He used to work in the commission for regulations. On the 15th of January, he was appointed the assistant for the enforcement of criminal and misdemeanour sanctions. For a while after that he performed his duty. As far as I know, because of the family reasons, at least that's what Karlo told me, he was the assistant for judiciary because of an illness in his family. I think it was his brother. He resigned. I really can't recall now until what time he worked, but it was for a while after his appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. If you would turn to P 0335 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, maybe I'm again stepping on your path, but a question you can certainly answer, Mr. Buntic. Did you, yourself, when you were appointed head of the department and took that office, did you pass an oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not and I don't think that any other head did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is P 03350, same binder. Mr. Buntic, do you recognise this as a work report that you made that sets out the work of the department of justice and general administration from the period of 1 January to 31 June 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph 1 right at the beginning of it makes a reference to Aid Glavovic having been relieved of his duties and having been replaced by Mr. Dragan Barbaric. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you don't indicate here when he was relieved of his duties. Do you recall when that took place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already indicated that I cannot remember when it was, and I told you why. First of all, the information I received from my deputy was that because of an illness in his family Mr. Glavovic was not at work. So the time when he stopped coming to work is different from the time when he was relieved of his duties. It was probably at a later date. I cannot be very specific here, but I think that Mr. Barbaric was not appointed before June or -- well, late May or early June as the assistant, and that may have been -- well, first you had to relieve Mr. Glavovic and then appoint Mr. Barbaric, and I think that this procedure whereby Mr. Glavovic was relieved of his duties and Mr. Dragan Barbaric appointed in his place, I think it was in late May or early June.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Buntic, the next exhibit, although I'm not -- you can look at it if you want. I'm not going to require you to do so, but I'm just going to put this to you and you can comment. I'm looking at P 10517, which is going to be in the fourth binder. And while that's being found, Mr. Buntic, representatives of my office interviewed Mr. Glavovic back in the year 2000 after you testified in the Kordic case. And he gave us a witness statement, and in the witness statement which he signed he states that the main reason why he decided to quit his work with the department of justice and administration of the HZ HB was his disagreement with their policy of requiring an oath of allegiance from their employees. This is the second paragraph page 3 of the English version. He said: "The oath was to be taken for the HZ HB, not the legitimate authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina." He said the oath was compulsory and that since he considered himself a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina he refused to take the oath. He gave the names of two other Muslim employees of the department of justice who also left the department on this question. He states that the oath-taking ceremony took place on the 22nd of January, 1993, which is the same date as the minutes that we just saw in which the oath -- the text of the oath for judges was approved. And he said this oath ceremony was presided over by Mr. Prlic. And so I'm just telling you that, I'm putting it to you, isn't that true that what really happened in respect of Mr. Glavovic, he left the department of justice because he declined to take a compulsory oath?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that my assistant, Glavovic, at one point was no longer working in the department, but everything else is incorrect. It is not correct that he was asked to make any kind of declaration because no head and no assistant to the head was ever asked to make such a declaration. As you can see, there were ten dozen of them and nobody was asked to do that. The same goes for my assistant Mr. Glavovic, and it is absolutely incorrect that Mr. Semir Puzic and Mr. Jugo Mahmut were also officials in the judiciary because they were judges in the division of the Supreme Court and evidence has been called before this Tribunal. We have decisions appointing them to the division or office of the Supreme Court, both of them. Now, I don't know how you were able to obtain this statement from Aid, but Aid Glavovic would never sign such a statement with all his wits about him. He is a fair and correct person, and in order to sign such a statement he must have been under duress. There must have been threats involved. I don't know what threats were used, but this is definitely not correct and this is definitely not accurate, this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is my last question on this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that Mr. Glavovic and his family were expelled from their home in west Mostar on the 9th of May, 1993, they had to flee over to the east side of the river, where they were still living in 2002 at the time he gave this statement? Do you know that's what became of him and his family?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that. I spoke to Aid after that. He told me about that. I'm really sorry this happened, but as I've already said my deputy was also captured in this action on the 9th of May, Karlo Sesar, he's a Croat. He's not a Muslim at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No further questions on this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 20 to 6.00. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I can direct you to the next exhibit, which is 1D 01978 which is in binder number 4. I think the next several documents are in this binder number 4. I'm going to stay a little bit longer with the courts and the prosecutors, as I was asking you about before the break. You indicated in your direct testimony that at various times reports were made. You made reports, you were forwarding reports, I think, of others on the work of these -- the various courts, civilian and district military courts. And do you recognise this exhibit, 1978, as a report made by the president of the district military court in Mostar, Mr. Maric, dated the 8th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it relates, looking at the very first sentence, to the first half of 1993 as the reporting period, and I want to -- go ahead, sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Directing you to the first sentence of the third paragraph, it states as follows: "The Court's priority task is to institute proceedings for crimes resulting from the Muslim aggression. Subsequently, proceedings have been instituted against the commander and other members of Muslim units from Mostar and other places for the crime of armed rebellion under Article 124 ...of the criminal code ...of the former Yugoslavia ..." And then it continues with the specification of additional crimes. Then I'm going to move down a few more lines to the reference to the crime of instigating an aggressive war under Article 152 of the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia. Now, first of all, here this being 8th of July, 1993, is it your recollection, sir, as indicated in this report that the priority of courts in this period -- or this particular court, I should say, was to institute proceedings for crimes related to Muslim aggression, as it's written here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the opinion, as you can see from this, of a president of a court, it is his report. I don't recall -- or in fact I can state quite categorically that I did not issue any such orders making this a priority. Now, whether the president received any such orders from anyone else, I don't know that. Perhaps this is just his independent opinion. So I can state quite categorically that no such order or instruction was ever issued by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me, sir, that the reference here to the crime of armed rebellion, for me, sir, that implies a crime in which a state is a victim; that is, it's a crime that is directed against a state. And so the reference here to armed rebellion, isn't that, sir, being instituted as a proceeding based on armed rebellion against the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only assume but -- or speculate what the president of this court thought when he wrote this report. I cannot give you any reliable testimony on this. I don't think it would be proper for me to speculate as to what the president of this court thought when he drafted this report. It is his report, it was submitted as such, forwarded. His views are presented in it, his opinions, and it is not up to me to comment it now, to comment it then, I never did comment. I never interfered with the independence of the courts or their decision-making. So I think that this follows from a number of my acts and documents that I drafted at the time. The decisions of the court, I as head of the department could not comment on those decisions and I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now then at the end of this paragraph this investigation for instigating an aggressive war, would you agree with me, sir, that the crime of aggression or aggressive war also implies actions taken against a state?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you that I should now try to divine what the president of the court thought. You have the document in front of you. It's a document drafted by the president of the district military court, so please don't ask me to comment on the court decisions. Because in principle, I always advocated the view that nobody should comment it. It was my opinion at the time. I expressed it in a number of documents and I confirm it here before this Tribunal. I don't want to change it in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The president of the court, Mr. Maric, was he approved by the HVO HZ HB to this position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. He was elected the president of the district military court after Mr. Enes Memic resigned, I believe, and then Mr. Velimir Maric was appointed. I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that in appointing Mr. Maric to this position the HVO was satisfied of his legal qualifications in order to take this position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Velimir Maric has a law degree and that he has appropriate education that would enable him to perform the duties of a judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we get to the next question, Your Honour, just -- I didn't object because I thought that the gentleman was entitled to his answers, but I do object to the Prosecution's interpretation on the law, what is meant by the crime of aggression as being against a state or armed rebellion. It would have been interesting to have asked Mr. Buntic what happened on, I believe, the late part of June. This may -- we all know, that must be -- I mean, you laugh, but being killed in your sleep is not a joking matter, Your Honour. I don't -- I'm sure that the victims of those -- of that aggression by their mates was not a laughing matter and maybe that's the armed rebellion that's being referred to. If the Prosecutor had known the facts maybe he would have put that question to the gentleman and ask him what happened on that particular evening. In other ways, Ms. Alaburic refers to it as a treacherous act. We can term it in various different ways. What I do object are the Prosecution's characterizations these crimes, as they're related here, go against the state, therefore trying to imply that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was posing as a state. In keeping with my objection, I would invite the Trial Chamber to look at these articles that are being referenced because I think that's what the judge is looking at, and I do agree with Mr. Buntic because I did notice a particular facial expression that he is being asked to divine what this gentleman meant. If the Prosecution wishes, they can call this person as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I agree with your last point, I had the same reaction, we should look at the paragraph, at the article of the law to see what it is. I apologise if I showed signs of a certain hilarity, it was only because some time ago one of your colleagues advised the Prosecutor what questions he should ask and I commented on that and the same thing happening again. Repetition is, as Mr. Praljak certainly knows very well, an element of comedy. So I couldn't help it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not trying to give advice. I would have told the gentleman that had he listened, for instance, to my first -- to my own direct examination, it would not have been necessary to spend a half an hour on the oath. The gentleman was very clear. I try not to give this particular Prosecutor advice because I'm sure he's more experienced than I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I remain neutral on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Stringer, again. I would like to say the following, and it is of course not a testimony, but since the -- since Mr. Karnavas raised the issue of the aggression and since I have been dealing with international public law for now for a few decades, I am able to say -- I hope at least that the -- according to the definition which was adopted by the General Assembly in 1974 on the case of aggression, it is -- of course it could be established that aggression is being committed or could be committed against a state or a kind of state entity or a government entity, et cetera, because otherwise it wouldn't have the crime to be committed. If it were only against certain population, it would have been already genocide or anything else in terms of international humanitarian law. So it is my comment on this matter, but again I say that I do not want to go into a theoretical debate on the terms of aggression, but it is according to my knowledge I would be able to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge Prandler, but as you aptly pointed out, you have a few decades of experience in dealing with this area and I don't think that we can presume that somebody in Mostar may have the experience that you've had in dealing with the matter. That's why terms sometimes are being used perhaps in a very sloppy manner. I don't know. I think the articles would give us greater guidance, but I do take your point and I appreciate your observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, continuing with this document, I'm going to direct your attention to the second-to-the-last paragraph which is at the top of page 2 of the English version. Actually, I'll just start with the last sentence on the previous page beginning with this statement: "Basic prerequisite for the court to work successfully is unity. During the previous period there was no unity in the district military court in Mostar. "The circumstances were such that there were two political factions, HZ HB and the former BH. This resulted in an absurd situation where a part of the court implemented the general policy of the other political authorities, which is contrary to the one which established the court. A logical consequence of the situation is organizational problems ..." Now, Mr. Buntic, in your direct examination I believe it was this document that you referred to in which you indicated that the Muslim judges only showed up at the court on payday. And my question is this: Isn't it a fact that Muslim judges were declining or were reluctant to participate in the activities of the court because they were called upon to implement HZ HB policy and not the policy of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise and I don't want to disrupt my learned friend, but perhaps in relation to the representation that's just been put now by way of cross-examination, my learned friend can refer to the exact transcript regarding what the witness actually said regarding the Muslim judges and payday. I think perhaps it's not exactly -- it wasn't exactly put in the manner that my learned friend has attributed to the witness right now. So perhaps the reference to the transcript would be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I don't have it, Mr. President. I can come back to it. I'm happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Mr. Khan is right. According to what I remember - but I might be wrong - the witness stated that those judges would come on payday only without being there for the remainder of the time. That's all he said. Maybe we could have a look at the transcript, otherwise maybe the witness can tell us again what he stated earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think your recollection is the same as mine. If I expressed it differently, it wasn't my intent to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course there wasn't an intent. I'm not alleging any such thing against my learned friend. I have great respect for him. All I'm saying is I think that there was, for my recollection, some dispute. My recollection may be faulty, my learned friend's may be faulty. In light of that ambiguity, I would ask that the actual portion of the transcript be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps there is an easier way. Mr. Buntic, do you recall what you said in this respect? Maybe you remember better than we do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember what I said, but if it was recorded differently in the transcript. I thought some, I didn't say all of them, would only show up on payday. So this was not in reference to all the judges but only some judges, and I still stand by that. I don't know whether the Prosecutor is going to ask the question again or to answer the question that was already asked. I don't know if you've completed your question, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll find the quote, Mr. President. And I'm looking -- we have it. I'm looking at page 30488 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you're describing this document, Mr. Buntic, it's a report of the district military court which was supposed to submit its reports to both the department of defence and the department of justice. You said: "I assume the responsibility for the work of all the judges in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna but do not take responsibility for the work of the judges appointed by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." You said: "The reason why is that these judges appeared in court only once a month when it was payday and we see that from this report." That's the top of 30488. So I'll take you back to my question referring to the text that I read earlier, which is this: Isn't it true, sir, that the judges, the Muslims judges or those appointed by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were unwilling to implement the policies of the HVO as indicated by Mr. Maric on this report --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again I'm going to object. Now he's mixing it up. Now he's saying the Muslim judges or those appointed by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, earlier he doesn't make any distinction. Somehow the Prosecutor is trying to show -- establish that Mr. Buntic is prejudiced or at least he's made some allegations against Muslim judges vis-a-vis other judges. He said those that were appointed by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, Mr. Buntic never said that those judges were all Muslim, nor did he say that those judges that would show up once were only Muslim. So I would expect the gentleman to put his question forthrightly. What exactly is he trying to say? But if he's going to quote from a text, he better quote accurately or I'm going to keep objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, judges - and I'll quote the text here that were -- well, there were two political factions according to Mr. Maric here, the HZ HB faction and the faction of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. My question is this, sir: You're making reference to judges appointed by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Isn't it a fact, sir, that they didn't participate in the court because they were opposed to implementing the policy that's referred here -- by Mr. Maric, the general policy of the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is the same as it -- as the one that I gave you before. I was thinking about the persons appointed by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not judges of Muslim ethnicity. I still say that those persons did very little work in the courts where they were appointed, and as you can see from this report - because my answer had to do with this report - the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina had appointed three judges to the district military court. It is true that all three judges appointed by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina were Bosniaks, and it was up to the HZ HB organs to appoint others. It is visible from this report that after the conflict, the war broke out between Bosniaks and Croats in Mostar, that those judges no longer came to work, no longer performed their jobs. I can agree with that part, and I think that it corresponded to the actual situation, state of affairs, in Mostar. So after the war broke out, the judges appointed by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina no longer came to work and they did not perform their tasks in court. But I still maintain that what I said can in no way apply to all the other judges of the Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Buntic, what you've just said is inconsistent with the last paragraph of this report of Mr. Maric in which he states that: "After the combat operations in Mostar on 9 May 1993, complete unity of the court was established in a short time. All organizational and personnel problems are taken in stride, without any major problems in spite of the war." So in fact isn't that really what happened, in that after the war broke out the judges who were not supportive of HZ HB policy were removed from the court and were replaced by judges who were supportive of HZ HB policy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody was removed from the court, by no decision of any organ or body of the HZ HB. Some people left their jobs, the post which they were appointed by a decision of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina voluntarily. They did so of their own will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, sorry, I have a question still with regard to this report. There is something that puzzles me a bit. The first sentence quoted by Mr. Stringer on the first page in the third paragraph says that: "The courts" -- and I quote: "The court's priority task is to institute proceedings for crimes ..." et cetera. Now, I'm a bit puzzled. Normally it is not the task of the court to institute proceedings. Could you explain this language? I guess that there is an explanation, but I will -- would like you to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot, Your Honour. I've already said that this was the position taken by the president of this court. I can share it or not share it, that's a completely different matter. But this is a report by the president of the district military court in Mostar and it was written --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I fully disagree. This is not an opinion or something. This is a report, and it starts out saying that: "The court's priority task is to institute proceedings ..." Now, you were the chief of the department of justice, you were responsible for courts, and you, I think, should know in your position what the task of a court is. And to me the task of a court normally is not that, to institute proceedings. I see Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic wants to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to assist, that's one of the things that I'm perhaps not so familiar with. I'm not familiar with the Swiss judiciary, but I am familiar with the Croatian judiciary and the Croatian Law on Criminal Procedure which was adopted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... are you the witness now or an expert under oath?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I merely wanted to tell you what the term "to institute" means. In our criminal procedure that doesn't mean filing a criminal report because under our Law on Criminal Procedure, the criminal proceedings are not instituted at the moment when criminal report is filed. That's what I wanted to say. I think that we have this law on the record, but I just wanted to tell you at one -- at what point criminal proceedings start. That's not at the moment when the criminal report is filed. I'm not going to say what's the document instituting criminal proceedings because this gentleman is a lawyer and he can tell us that, but this is just a technical legal matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this report seems to be a report from the president of the military court. This is not a civilian court. This is a report coming from a military court. Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. And there is a difference between a civilian judge and a military judge. A civilian judge is "more independent" than a military judge or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the regulations that were in force, that were applied, that's what follows, that civilian courts are independent in their work, whereas the organization and structure of military courts was somewhat different, both during the times of the former Yugoslavia, and we can see that from the regulations governing the status of military prosecutor's offices and the courts and that all was adopted by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This military judge has prepared this report, but based on his own area which is to deal with military-type crimes, desertions, rebellions. Here we have a report that deals with crimes committed within the military jurisdiction, and as far as I understand - but you will correct me if I'm wrong - the proceedings are instigated by the military prosecutor based on reports prepared by the military police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how it should have been according to the regulations that were in force in the territory of the HZ HB, but as for the priorities in work on cases, the president of the court decided that. I'm not saying anything new. We know that from prior practice. The president of the court, depending on the workload and the type of cases, decides on what the priorities were going to be. It doesn't mean that in some other court a different president wouldn't decide otherwise. That's why I said, this is the opinion of this president of the court on the priorities of that court. I also said that he never received any instructions from me as to priorities. It is in the discretion of the president to set out priorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But since he was presiding over military-type cases, were you in a position to give instructions to him or did it have nothing to do with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not give any instructions, and according to regulations I was not able to give any. It was up to the president, and I said I gave presidents no instructions. It is up to the president to decide what the priorities are going to be at a given moment. That is within his authority. All the powers in that sense are vested in the president, and he decided on that independently. And it doesn't mean necessarily that some other court didn't have different priorities. To interfere with that part of the work, in my eyes, would have been interference with the work of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A linguistic question, Mr. Buntic, because we have insisted a lot on the words. In Croatian does "institute proceedings" and "decide on priorities" mean the same thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it does not. But whether it is just a slip or the actual opinion and position of this president is not up to me to decide or make any statements about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, the next exhibit is 1D 01974, and this is a report that you made on the work of the courts, district courts, military courts for Mostar and Livno municipalities dated the 5th of August, 1993. Do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so in this report what you're reporting on are statistics, the activities of the district court in Mostar, district military prosecutor Mostar, district court Livno, district military prosecutor Livno, also Travnik district military court. And I see that in the first section on the district court in Mostar you indicate in your report that for the first quarter, 1993, most requests to conduct an investigation pertain to Serbs from the territory of the municipalities of Capljina, Stolac, Neum, and Mostar for the crime of serving in an enemy army, while in the second quarter the situation changed considerably following the armed aggression of the Muslim army on units in the HVO, namely, in the aforementioned period, a large number of reports were received by members of the Muslim army for the following crimes: Armed rebellion, genocide, war crimes against civilians, war crimes against prisoners of war, war crimes against the sick and wounded and then instigating an aggressive war. And then you continue in your report you're providing statistics on the cases, making reference to the K numbers that you described for us during your cross-examination by counsel for Mr. Coric. You go on to describe or to report on statistics for the district military prosecutor's office in Mostar at the bottom of page 2 of the English version. These are reports of -- well, let me ask you. At the top of the table there's an indication that there were 652 reports that were received, and those reports indicated or reported crimes alleged to have been committed by 2.691 people. Is that a correct interpretation, 652 reports of crimes that pertained to 2.691 alleged criminals or perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a compound question. This is an aggregated report made up of all the reports filed by courts --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- anything else than the figures provided by courts, it would be wrong to say anything about that. All we can do is do the math.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are all the reports from all the courts in that area. You can tell me that I did the math wrong, you can hold that against me, but anything else --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, I -- excuse me --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The qualifications given and denominations of various acts are just taken over from those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I understand that you're simply forwarding on the reports that you're receiving from the courts. We understand that. However, sir, this is your report. It appears over your signature. I think it's fair for us to assume that a gentleman holding the position that you held at the time, that you knew what you were talking about when you reported about the reports of armed rebellion or the reports of aggressive war. I mean, you knew or you must have had some idea what those crimes involved at the time you made this report; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. However, it is not correct that I was able to change the qualifications assigned by the courts, and it's not a report. It's just information. I could not modify the qualification of a crime. I copied it as it was written in the report by the court. I didn't sign it, actually it's my deputy who signed but it's the same thing. Neither he nor I were able to change the legal qualification given by the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I understand that --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as I can't change the legal qualifications you assign to a certain crime. You should be fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, if you'll allow me, sir, I'm not suggesting that you could have changed these qualifications. I'm not suggesting that in the least. I'm simply asking you what you were talking about or what your understanding of armed rebellion and aggressive war was when you reported these investigations.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have stated already, this is not a report. This is a piece of information, that's one. Two, this is not my opinion. This is information provided by courts and legal qualifications assigned by courts. Now you're asking me why didn't I change the qualifications assigned by the courts, well, who would I have been to do that? The question arises: Who would I have to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's move to the next document, Mr. Buntic, 1D 02004. Now, this is a document, I believe, issued by you on the following day, the 6th of August, 1993. And again, I recognise you're just reporting on the information that you're receiving from the other courts referred to in this document. This appears to be your report on the work of municipal misdemeanour courts, district military prosecutor's offices, district military courts in the HZ HB for the period 1 January 1993 to 6 August 1993; is that correct? Do you have that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but I want to say this --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I get to ask the questions. We'll make time for you to make a statement, but only after I've had my time to ask you my questions, sir. In this report I am going to refer you to item number 3, and, again, I understand that you're simply reporting or repeating the information that's come to you from the various courts. In the second paragraph under item 3, you're reporting on the information from the municipal court for misdemeanours in Livno. Do you see that? "Municipal court for misdemeanours in Livno did not receive a single request from the defence office ..." Do you see that part?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then this paragraph continues down. There's a reference to the municipal court for misdemeanours in Tomislavgrad. Continuing down, there's a reference to the municipal court for misdemeanours in Citluk. And then about halfway through the paragraph there's a reference to the municipal court for misdemeanours in Mostar. Do you see that? "... Mostar received from the defence department -- the defence office 318 requests ..." Do you see that text?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so just to make sure, we're talking about the Mostar municipal court for misdemeanours, and you're talking about the president of the court. And I take it, sir, the president of that court was your source of information here on the activities of this court. He stated that: "A large number of cases could not be completed due to the parties being beyond reach because some of the reports concerned persons of Muslim ethnicity for whom confirmations issued by the army of BH are recognised according to the official letter of the defence office ..." And then you say in your report that: "He," the president of the court, " ...pointed out the fact that a large number of Muslims had been taken away from their current addresses so it was impossible to serve summons." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this is the 6th of August, 1993. At this period in time, Mr. Buntic, is it correct that hundreds of Muslims throughout western Herzegovina were being removed from their homes and their flats, not just in Mostar but in other municipalities as well. And the men, the Muslim men of military age were being taken to camps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croats, too, were removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My question is a different one, isn't it? I'm asking you whether hundreds of Muslims were being evicted from their homes and their flats throughout the Mostar region at this period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's your question and this is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm waiting for your answer. I think it's a yes or a no or an I don't know.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered as I answered. It's true that both Croats and Muslims were removed, but it's not true that only Muslims were being removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So when the reference in this paragraph is to large numbers of Muslims being taken away, that's a reference, isn't it, sir, to them being taken away by the HVO and put in camps or otherwise being driven away from their homes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Similarly, it is believed that those Croats who were removed were taken away by the BH army, and it's equally true that it is considered in relation to the Muslims who were removed that they were taken away by the HVO and other Croat units in that area. But you can't ask a lop-sided question like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These things happened on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that's the reason why the process, the legal procedures that are being referred to here, weren't working. Muslims, as he's saying here, he's talking about Muslims. He's not talking about Croats. The president of the court's talking about Muslims who can't be served with the papers because they've been taken away; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is taken from the higher court of misdemeanours in Mostar, but I stand by my answer, namely, that the situation was similar on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, does that make it legitimate on either side? Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that, Mr. Prosecutor, by no means. I'm just stating the facts that we all knew, all of us who were from that area, and you cannot just say one-sidedly that Muslims were being removed without mentioning that Croats were being removed too. They were removed just before and during the conflict, but throughout the war 5.000 Muslims continued to live in the Croat-controlled area, whereas only 74 Croats continued throughout the war to live in the Muslim-controlled area. And now it is up to the Court to make a judgement as to who was responsible for more removals of people, not you. It is up to the Court to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next document that -- it's actually not in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm sorry, Mr. Stringer, but my attention is drawn to all sorts of things. Mr. Buntic, in the large paragraph on the second page we read that: "The municipal court for misdemeanours in Tomislavgrad received 333 misdemeanour reports ..." And the end of the next line: " ...all the cases were archived based on the decision of the municipal HVO." Now, I would like to know how this is to be interpreted, but it looks as if the executive of the municipality interfered with the work of the local municipal court, which was perhaps ever so happy to have less work but that is not the issue here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is obvious, Your Honour, because it followed from this report that the municipal HVO instructed the president of the court to act on these cases as he did act. If we look at that report that came from the higher court for misdemeanours which informs us that it was the way it was done in Tomislavgrad and we only received information that this was happening. I think this is consistent with the information received from the municipal misdemeanours court in Tomislavgrad. Yes, it does follow that somebody from the HVO gave those instructions to the president of the court, but you have to bear in mind that municipal misdemeanour courts were courts established by the municipality. The municipality appoints the judge, the judge is answerable to the municipality, and the court is financed from the municipal budget. So not a single body of the HZ HB had jurisdiction over municipal misdemeanour courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I let that stand. Excuse me, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, I'm at a bit of a breaking point here. I know it's a few minutes early, but it might be better in the long run if we could break for the evening now rather than moving into the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer, how much time do you need tomorrow to complete?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think as much time as I have remaining and possibly some more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar will tell us how much time you have left. I'll tell you precisely, but I believe it's around one hour. I'm being told that you've used six hours and 37 minutes. You had been granted seven hours and 15 minutes. In other words, you have less than an hour left. Witness, as you know, you will return here tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m., of course. We won't finish at midnight, and we should be able, since we start in the morning, we should be able to complete your testimony in the morning as well. I wish you all a pleasant evening and we'll meet again in this courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 18th day of July, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.56 p.m.,
